HaldenBuilds

the exact prompts, typos and all

One prompt. Three films.

Three finished motion graphics films, each made by Claude Opus 5.5 from one typed brief in one unattended run. The prompts are here word for word, so you can copy one and point it at your own business.

One-shot means one brief in and one finished film out, with no back and forth.

TypeWhat we changedFilm
SIMPLENothing. The prompt as typed, with no references.45 seconds
MIDDLEAsked for outlandish. Banned references. Added a paragraph on transitions.60 seconds
INSPIREDAsked for outlandish. Let it study public reels first.60 seconds

What it took

Each brief ran in Claude Code, where the model writes and runs code on the computer. The two runs we timed took 1 hour 41 minutes (SIMPLE) and 2 hours 47 minutes (INSPIRED), start to finish, unattended.

What every brief also set

The length. Three sizes: 4K wide, 1080p wide, and a vertical cut laid out on its own. Original music and sound, with no voice. A list of checks the model ran on its own files before it stopped.

SIMPLE

Type 1 of 3The prompt alone. No references given.

What we asked

We typed one message and sent it. The model got no reference clips, no style guide and no storyboard. It chose its own tools, wrote the film as code, rendered it and checked it.

The prompt, word for word · quoted from the brief that made this film

The prompt, exactly as typed

I heard Opus 5.5 was excellent at motions graphics. I need a SoTA cutting-edge motion graphics presentation of how great and sophisticated Opus 5.5 is at this.
The video should be about how great it is and how it does it, if possible breaking down its own process from start to finish to create such amazing motion graphics that enterprises would pay tens of thousands of dollars for, but it does it for *insert the amount of input/output - or total tokens AND % usage in the 5-hour limit (with the help of the orchestrator session*
They told me I didn't have to give you any references because you're great at it.
Don't stop until your finished, it should be 45-secounds long.
Note: If you don't know exactly what your process is, probably start a part of it that you're clear on, and start breaking down your workflow, appraoch and process that way (or maybe with just that you'd have it figured out)
PS: Also write down a full report, manifest and breakdown of the workflow and engines/scripts/etc that you used us to replicate it with less usage in the future - but don't mention this in the video itself
I'd assume you know and would do QA QC on your work

The prompt's second line names a price. It is part of the brief as typed, quoted unchanged.

A frame from the SIMPLE film.

What came out

A 45 second film at 60 frames a second, in three sizes. It walks through its own making in six numbered steps, from reading the brief to checking the render. The still is the title, at 6.5 seconds.

Transitions note

This prompt never mentions transitions. Add the paragraph below before you send it.

Transitions between sections. Design every section boundary as its own beat. Carry an element, a shape, a color, a camera move or a sound across the cut, so the viewer is pulled from one idea into the next. When the film is done, list every boundary with the device you used and a frame pair that shows it.

Added: outlandish

So: the same brief, pushed much further. Outlandish means bolder concepts, stranger transitions, more daring type and motion than a safe corporate reel, while staying legible and finished.

Added: no research

**No research (his ruling JI-522.90, the middle ground):** you may NOT look for references or inspiration anywhere: no web, no video tools on outside clips, no Pinterest, no YouTube. Everything comes from your own judgment, like film 1, but pushed outlandish.

Added: transitions

**Transitions between sequences/sections.** The motion graphics inside each section were strong in the earlier films; the hand-off from one section to the next is where they were weaker. Design every section boundary as its own beat: carry an element, a shape, a colour, a camera move or a sound across the cut so the viewer is pulled from one idea into the next, never dropped. In REPORT.md, list every section boundary with the device you used and a frame pair showing it.

Use it for your brand or business

We ran the same method on a brand. That brief named HaldenBuilds, pointed at its colors, typefaces and approved lines, and set the same length, sizes, sound and checks. Your film starts the same way.

One prompt into your own film

  1. Swap the subject. Replace the first two lines of the prompt with yours. Say what the film is about, who it is for and how long it runs. Three starters are on the right.
  2. Hand over your brand kit. Your colors as exact codes. The font files you are licensed to use. Your logo as an SVG. Three to five lines you already say about the business, to be used as the words on screen.
  3. Pick a type. SIMPLE to see what the model does alone. MIDDLE for a bolder film built from nothing outside. INSPIRED when there are reels you admire: it studies them and copies none.
  4. Set the practical parts. The length. The sizes, with the vertical cut laid out on its own. Original music and sound. Then the floors our briefs used: main words at least 9% of the screen's short side, contrast at least 7 to 1, and every line held still for 0.4 seconds per word plus 0.6.
  5. Ask it to check its own files. The length, the spelling of every word on screen, and a read test at phone width. After that, change anything with a sentence, such as: slow the second part down.
  6. Keep the code. The first film leaves a folder of code that holds your colors, fonts and scene types. That folder is your render library. Start the next film from it.

The same method on a brand

One frame of the HaldenBuilds film, at 13.2 seconds. The line on it is the brand's own.

Three starters

Explainer

I need a 45 second motion graphics film that explains [what you do] to [who buys it].

Launch

I need a 30 second motion graphics film that announces [product] and shows the three things it does.

Product

I need a 60 second motion graphics film that walks through [product] step by step, from start to finish.

Re-cut video you already have

The same approach edits finished video. Claude writes the edit as commands for ffmpeg, an open-source video tool, and draws titles and captions in code on top. Ask for cuts, captions timed from a transcript, a size for each platform, and even loudness.

Done here. Each film in this guide had one segment replaced and all three sizes joined again by a script, with no new render of the rest. Each soundtrack was measured for loudness.

Still to do. A full edit of filmed footage. We have not run one yet.

Finish it in After Effects

Once the render library exists, a scene can be exported as separate layers and taken into After Effects for hand finishing: a timing change, a mask, a color pass.

Done, on disk

One scene exported as three layers: the ground, the picture and the words. Each is ProRes 4444 video, 1080 by 1920, 60 frames long. The picture and words layers have transparent backgrounds. The words layer also exists as 60 PNG files.

Carries over

The pixels, the timing and the transparency of every layer. Each layer arrives as its own clip, so it can be handled on its own.

Does not carry over

The controls. A layer that arrives as video is pixels. Its words cannot be retyped there and its motion curve cannot be reshaped there. For that kind of change, change the code and export again.

Untested

Opening the layers in After Effects. It is not installed on the machine that made them. A script that would rebuild a simple scene with live text and keyframes is written from Adobe's scripting guide and has not had its first run.

Your next step

Give Claude your Foundations Kit, then brief your first film.

The kit came with this guide. It holds the files Claude reads before it starts: who you serve, what you sell, your pricing. Write the brief in that same session, and the first two lines of your prompt can point at those files.

How

  1. Unzip the kit and open the folder in Claude Code.
  2. Paste this one line:
    Read KIT-MANIFEST.md in this folder and follow its notice to the recipient's agent.
  3. Copy a prompt from this guide, swap its first two lines for your business, and send it.

How this was made

Each film came from one typed brief and one unattended run in Claude Code. A script copied the prompts on these pages from those briefs and compared them character for character, so every typo is the original. Each still is one frame of its film.

Building leverage, the right way.
